notes.front: What is an inline sensor?
notes.back: An IDPS sensor deployed so that the network traffic it monitors must pass through it.
notes.explanation: Because traffic flows through it, as it would through a firewall, an inline sensor is in a position to block traffic and so stop attacks.
notes.example: Like a ticket barrier every passenger must walk through, rather than a guard watching the crowd from a balcony.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 4.2.2 Network Architectures and Sensor Locations, p. 38
notes.evidence: An inline sensor is deployed so that the network traffic it is monitoring must pass through it, much like the traffic flow associated with a firewall.

notes.front: What is a passive sensor?
notes.back: An IDPS sensor that monitors a copy of the actual network traffic; no traffic passes through it.
notes.explanation: It watches a duplicate of the traffic, so it sits beside the flow rather than in it.
notes.example: Like a security camera filming a corridor: it sees everyone go by but cannot close a door on anyone.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 4.2.2 Network Architectures and Sensor Locations, p. 39
notes.evidence: A passive sensor is deployed so that it monitors a copy of the actual network traffic; no traffic actually passes through the sensor.

notes.front: In NIST’s zero trust architecture, what is the control plane used for?
notes.back: Maintaining and configuring assets; judging, granting or denying access; and setting up communication paths between resources.
notes.explanation: It is used by infrastructure components, whether enterprise-owned or from service providers.
notes.example: Like air traffic control: it clears and routes flights but carries no passengers itself.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, 3.4 Network Requirements, p. 30
notes.evidence: The control plane is used by various infrastructure components (both enterprise-owned and from service providers) to maintain and configure assets; judge, grant, or deny access to resources; and perform any necessary operations to set up communication paths between resources.

notes.front: In NIST’s zero trust architecture, what is the data plane used for?
notes.back: The actual communication between software components.
notes.explanation: The organisation’s actual work, software talking to software, travels here.
notes.example: Like the aircraft that carry passengers along the routes air traffic control has cleared.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, 3.4 Network Requirements, p. 30
notes.evidence: The data plane is used for actual communication between software components.

notes.front: What is out-of-band management?
notes.back: Managing systems over a channel separate from the in-band paths that carry routine operational traffic, such as a physically separate network.
notes.explanation: NIST lists network paths physically separate from operational ones, and local non-network access, among out-of-band channels.
notes.example: Like a building’s maintenance staircase: staff reach the plant room without using the public lifts.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-37 Out-of-Band Channels, p. 350
notes.evidence: Out-of-band channels include local, non-network accesses to systems; network paths physically separate from network paths used for operational traffic; or non-electronic paths, such as the U.S. Postal Service. The use of out-of-band channels is contrasted with the use of in-band channels (i.e., the same channels) that carry routine operational traffic.

notes.front: What is an application-proxy gateway?
notes.back: A feature of advanced firewalls: a proxy agent acts as an intermediary between two hosts and never allows a direct connection between them.
notes.explanation: It combines lower-layer access control with upper-layer functionality.
notes.example: Like a receptionist who takes a visitor’s message and carries it upstairs, so the visitor never meets the staff member directly.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.4 Application-Proxy Gateways, p. 16
notes.evidence: An application-proxy gateway is a feature of advanced firewalls that combines lower-layer access control with upper-layer functionality. These firewalls contain a proxy agent that acts as an intermediary between two hosts that wish to communicate with each other, and never allows a direct connection between them.

notes.front: In NIST, what is a dedicated proxy server?
notes.back: A server that relays one application’s traffic, such as email or web, as a proxy, with much more limited firewalling than an application-proxy gateway.
notes.explanation: It keeps proxy control of traffic but little of a firewall’s filtering role.
notes.example: Like a post room that screens and logs parcels but relies on the building’s security gate to keep intruders out.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.5 Dedicated Proxy Servers, p. 16
notes.evidence: Dedicated proxy servers differ from application-proxy gateways in that while dedicated proxy servers retain proxy control of traffic, they usually have much more limited firewalling capabilities.

notes.front: What is a web application firewall (WAF)?
notes.back: A specialised application firewall that sits in front of a web server and detects exploits of the protocol web servers use.
notes.explanation: Many, not necessarily all, such exploits can be caught this way.
notes.example: Like a doorman who checks every order handed to a restaurant’s kitchen, not just who walks in.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.9 Web Application Firewalls, p. 19
notes.evidence: Many of these exploits can be detected by specialized application firewalls called web application firewalls that reside in front of the web server.

notes.front: What is a cloud access security broker (CASB)?
notes.back: Software that sits on the network between cloud service customers and cloud service providers.
notes.explanation: NIST calls it one of the most important pieces of software for enterprises that subscribe to multiple clouds.
notes.example: Like a customs post between a company and its many cloud suppliers, checking what crosses in each direction.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB), p. 17
notes.evidence: Given the increasing subscription to multiple clouds in many enterprises, one of the most important pieces of software is the cloud access security broker (CASB). It sits on the network between the cloud service customers (CSC) and the cloud service providers (CSP).

notes.front: What is signature-based detection?
notes.back: Comparing signatures (patterns that correspond to known threats) against observed events to identify possible incidents.
notes.explanation: A signature describes something already known to be bad, so a match flags a possible incident.
notes.example: Like a shop guard with a folder of photographs of known shoplifters.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 2.3.1 Signature-Based Detection, p. 18
notes.evidence: A signature is a pattern that corresponds to a known threat. Signature-based detection is the process of comparing signatures against observed events to identify possible incidents.

notes.front: What is anomaly-based detection?
notes.back: Comparing definitions of normal activity against observed events to identify significant deviations.
notes.explanation: The IDPS holds profiles of the normal behaviour of users, hosts, connections or applications and looks for departures from them.
notes.example: Like a bank noticing that a customer who always spends locally has suddenly made ten purchases abroad.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 2.3.2 Anomaly-Based Detection, p. 18
notes.evidence: Anomaly-based detection is the process of comparing definitions of what activity is considered normal against observed events to identify significant deviations. An IDPS using anomaly-based detection has profiles that represent the normal behavior of such things as users, hosts, network connections, or applications.

notes.front: What is stateful protocol analysis?
notes.back: Comparing predetermined profiles of benign protocol activity, for each protocol state, against observed events to identify deviations.
notes.explanation: The comparison is made separately for each state a protocol can be in.
notes.example: Like a referee who knows which moves are legal at each stage of a game and blows the whistle at an out-of-turn move.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 2.3.3 Stateful Protocol Analysis, p. 19
notes.evidence: Stateful protocol analysis is the process of comparing predetermined profiles of generally accepted definitions of benign protocol activity for each protocol state against observed events to identify deviations.

notes.front: What does a load balancer do?
notes.back: It distributes load across multiple instances of the same service.
notes.explanation: NIST gives distributing loads to services as load balancing’s main purpose.
notes.example: Like a supermarket attendant sending each shopper to the next free till.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-204, Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems, 4.5.2 Strategies for Load Balancing, p. 32
notes.evidence: its main purpose is to distribute loads to services. A service name is associated with a namespace that supports multiple instances of the same service.

notes.front: What is data loss prevention (DLP) technology used for?
notes.back: Automatically monitoring sensitive data, such as PII, internally or at network boundaries for unusual or suspicious transfers.
notes.explanation: NIST gives DLP technologies as an example of automated tools for information system monitoring of PII.
notes.example: Like a scanner at an office exit that flags anyone carrying out files stamped “confidential”.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-122, Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of PII, Information System Monitoring (SI-4), p. 31
notes.evidence: Organizations can employ automated tools to monitor PII internally or at network boundaries for unusual or suspicious transfers or events. An example is the use of data loss prevention technologies.

notes.front: What is a unified threat management (UTM) system?
notes.back: One system combining several features, typically a firewall, malware detection and eradication, and sensing and blocking of suspicious probes.
notes.explanation: It bundles several functions that would otherwise run on separate devices.
notes.example: Like a multi-tool: blade, screwdriver and scissors in one handle instead of three separate tools.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.8 Unified Threat Management (UTM), p. 19
notes.evidence: A typical unified threat management (UTM) system has a firewall, malware detection and eradication, sensing and blocking of suspicious network probes, and so on.

notes.front: Inline sensors are typically placed where network firewalls would be: at the {{c1::divisions between networks}}, such as connections with external networks.
notes.explanation: The borders between internal networks that should be kept apart are also named as typical inline locations.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 4.2.2 Network Architectures and Sensor Locations, p. 38
notes.evidence: Inline sensors are typically placed where network firewalls and other network security devices would be placed—at the divisions between networks, such as connections with external networks and borders between different internal networks that should be segregated.

notes.front: What is the primary motivation for deploying IDPS sensors inline?
notes.back: To let them stop attacks by blocking network traffic.
notes.explanation: NIST names blocking traffic, and so stopping attacks, as the main reason.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 4.2.2 Network Architectures and Sensor Locations, p. 38
notes.evidence: The primary motivation for deploying IDPS sensors inline is to enable them to stop attacks by blocking network traffic.

notes.front: Which switch port can see all the network traffic going through the switch, and so can feed a passive sensor?
notes.back: A spanning port.
notes.explanation: So a sensor connected there can observe all of the switch’s traffic.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 4.2.2 Network Architectures and Sensor Locations, p. 39
notes.evidence: Many switches have a spanning port, which is a port that can see all network traffic going through the switch.

notes.front: Why do passive sensors typically offer no reliable way to stop traffic reaching its destination?
notes.back: Because they monitor only a copy of the traffic.
notes.explanation: A passive sensor can sometimes inject packets to disrupt a connection, but NIST calls such methods generally less effective than inline ones.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 4.2.2 Network Architectures and Sensor Locations, p. 40
notes.evidence: Because passive techniques monitor a copy of the traffic, they typically provide no reliable way for a sensor to stop the traffic from reaching its destination. In some cases, a passive sensor can place packets onto a network to attempt to disrupt a connection, but such methods are generally less effective than inline methods.

notes.front: A team wants its new network IDPS to block attack traffic automatically, not just raise alerts. How should it deploy the sensors?
notes.back: B: inline, so traffic passes through them.
notes.choices:
A) Passive, on a spanning port
B) Inline, so traffic passes through them
C) Passive, on a network tap
D) On the management network only
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are passive methods: they see a copy of the traffic and typically cannot reliably stop it. D is where management servers and consoles connect, not where production traffic flows.
notes.explanation: NIST’s rule of thumb is inline when prevention methods will be used, passive when they will not.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 4.2.2 Network Architectures and Sensor Locations, p. 40
notes.evidence: Generally, organizations should deploy sensors inline if prevention methods will be used and passive if they will not.

notes.front: Which kind of IDPS sensor should an organisation deploy if it will not use prevention methods?
notes.back: A passive sensor.
notes.explanation: NIST ties the choice to whether the sensor is expected to block anything.
notes.contrast: An inline sensor is chosen when prevention methods will be used, because traffic must pass through it.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 4.2.2 Network Architectures and Sensor Locations, p. 40
notes.evidence: Generally, organizations should deploy sensors inline if prevention methods will be used and passive if they will not.

notes.front: Two virtual machines on the same physical host exchange traffic, yet the perimeter firewall logs none of it. Which fix does NIST’s firewall guide point to?
notes.back: C: use a firewall built into the virtualisation system, or a third-party plug-in firewall.
notes.choices:
A) Add more rules to the perimeter firewall
B) Move the perimeter firewall to a passive sensor
C) Use a firewall built into the virtualisation system, or a third-party plug-in firewall
D) Add a load balancer in front of the host
notes.choicesExplained: A cannot help: the traffic never reaches the external firewall. B and D do not place any control between the two machines.
notes.explanation: Traffic passing directly between virtualised operating systems within a host cannot be monitored by an external firewall.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.10 Firewalls for Virtual Infrastructures, p. 19
notes.evidence: Network activity that passes directly between virtualized operating systems within a host cannot be monitored by an external firewall. However, some virtualization systems offer built-in firewalls or allow third-party software firewalls to be added as plug-ins.

notes.front: Why does NIST break systems into separate subnets for different security domains?
notes.back: To give network connections to domains holding information of different security categories or classification levels the appropriate protection.
notes.explanation: Each subnet can then be protected to the level its information needs.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-7(22) Separate Subnets for Connecting to Different Security Domains, p. 330
notes.evidence: The decomposition of systems into subnetworks (i.e., subnets) helps to provide the appropriate level of protection for network connections to different security domains that contain information with different security categories or classification levels.

notes.front: What two benefits does NIST give for isolating system components that perform different business functions?
notes.back: It limits unauthorised information flows among components, and allows greater protection for selected components.
notes.explanation: The isolation applies to components performing different mission or business functions.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-7(21) Isolation of System Components, p. 329
notes.evidence: Organizations can isolate system components that perform different mission or business functions. Such isolation limits unauthorized information flows among system components and provides the opportunity to deploy greater levels of protection for selected system components.

notes.front: NIST says the separation of user functions from system management functions is {{c1::physical or logical}}.
notes.explanation: The control lists different computers, operating system instances, CPUs, network addresses or virtualisation as ways to separate them.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality, p. 320
notes.evidence: The separation of user functions from system management functions is physical or logical. Organizations may separate system management functions from user functions by using different computers, instances of operating systems, central processing units, or network addresses; by employing virtualization techniques

notes.front: In NIST, which plane must set up a communication path before the data plane can use it?
notes.back: The control plane.
notes.explanation: The policy administrator and PEP can set up the path over the control plane; the workload then uses the data-plane path.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, 3.4 Network Requirements, p. 30
notes.evidence: This communication channel may not be possible before the path has been established via the control plane. For example, the control plane could be used by the PA and PEP to set up the communication path between the subject and the enterprise resource.

notes.front: A zero trust policy administrator tells a gateway to allow a laptop to reach a payroll server. The laptop then uploads a timesheet to that server. Which plane carries the timesheet?
notes.back: C: the data plane.
notes.choices:
A) The control plane
B) The out-of-band plane
C) The data plane
D) The management plane
notes.choicesExplained: A carries the administrator’s instruction to set up the path, not the work traffic. B and D are not the planes NIST uses for this split.
notes.explanation: Application and service traffic between software components travels on the data plane.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, 3.4 Network Requirements, p. 30
notes.evidence: The data plane is used for actual communication between software components.

notes.front: What are two benefits of placing IDPS components on a separate management network?
notes.back: Concealing the IDPS from attackers; protecting it from attack; ensuring adequate bandwidth under adverse conditions (any two).
notes.explanation: The management network is isolated from the production networks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 3.1.2 Network Architectures, p. 24
notes.evidence: This architecture effectively isolates the management network from the production networks. The benefits of doing this are to conceal the existence and identity of the IDPS from attackers; to protect the IDPS from attack; and to ensure that the IDPS has adequate bandwidth to function under adverse conditions

notes.front: A small firm cannot afford a separate IDPS management network and puts management traffic on a VLAN instead. What does NIST say about this choice?
notes.back: B: it protects IDPS communications, but less than a separate management network.
notes.choices:
A) It gives the same protection as a separate management network
B) It protects IDPS communications, but less than a separate management network
C) It gives no protection at all
D) It is forbidden for IDPS deployments
notes.choicesExplained: A overstates it: a VLAN misconfiguration could expose IDPS data, and shared devices can saturate. C and D contradict the source, which offers the VLAN as a way to improve security.
notes.explanation: A misconfigured VLAN, for example, could expose IDPS data.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 3.1.2 Network Architectures, p. 24
notes.evidence: Using a VLAN provides protection for IDPS communications, but not as much protection as a separate management network. For example, misconfiguration of the VLAN could lead to the exposure of IDPS data.

notes.front: Why does an attack that compromises in-band channels not compromise out-of-band channels?
notes.back: Out-of-band channels do not have the same vulnerability or exposure as in-band channels.
notes.explanation: NIST draws the consequence for all three of confidentiality, integrity and availability.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-37 Out-of-Band Channels, p. 350
notes.evidence: Out-of-band channels do not have the same vulnerability or exposure as in-band channels. Therefore, the confidentiality, integrity, or availability compromises of in-band channels will not compromise or adversely affect the out-of-band channels.

notes.front: During a flood attack the production network is saturated, but engineers still reach the core routers’ management consoles over a physically separate cabled network. What is this an example of?
notes.back: C: out-of-band management.
notes.choices:
A) A data plane
B) Split tunnelling
C) Out-of-band management
D) A demilitarised zone
notes.choicesExplained: A carries the work traffic that is saturated. B is a remote-access VPN setting. D is a buffer network for public-facing services, not an admin path.
notes.explanation: A network path physically separate from operational traffic is an out-of-band channel, so the flood in-band does not affect it.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-37 Out-of-Band Channels, p. 350
notes.evidence: network paths physically separate from network paths used for operational traffic

notes.front: What does NIST’s control on separating system and user functionality require to be kept apart from user functionality?
notes.back: System management functionality.
notes.explanation: The control counts user interface services on the user side of that split.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality, p. 320
notes.evidence: Separate user functionality, including user interface services, from system management functionality.

notes.front: Under least functionality, where feasible, organisations limit component functionality to {{c1::a single function per component}}.
notes.explanation: Providing several services from one component is convenient, but NIST says it increases risk.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, CM-7 Least Functionality, p. 132
notes.evidence: it is sometimes convenient to provide multiple services from a single system component, but doing so increases risk over limiting the services provided by that single component. Where feasible, organizations limit component functionality to a single function per component.

notes.front: Under least functionality, what should organisations consider disabling to prevent unauthorised connection of components?
notes.back: Unused or unnecessary physical and logical ports and protocols.
notes.explanation: NIST names unauthorised connection, information transfer and tunnelling as what this prevents.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, CM-7 Least Functionality, p. 132
notes.evidence: Organizations consider removing unused or unnecessary software and disabling unused or unnecessary physical and logical ports and protocols to prevent unauthorized connection of components, transfer of information, and tunneling.

notes.front: An auditor finds that the IDPS sensors themselves run an out-of-date operating system with default services left on. What does NIST recommend?
notes.back: B: keep all components fully up to date and harden them.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: security devices are exempt from patching
B) Keep all components fully up to date and harden them
C) Replace signature-based with anomaly-based detection
D) Move the sensors to passive mode
notes.choicesExplained: A is the opposite of the advice. D changes placement, not the sensors’ weaknesses. C changes detection, not the sensors’ own security.
notes.explanation: NIST applies this to every component’s operating system and applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), Executive Summary, p. 9
notes.evidence: All components’ operating systems and applications should be kept fully up-to-date, and all software-based IDPS components should be hardened against threats.

notes.front: How many connections does each successful connection through an application-proxy gateway actually create?
notes.back: Two: client to proxy, and proxy to the true destination.
notes.explanation: The proxy sits in the middle of both connections.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.4 Application-Proxy Gateways, p. 16
notes.evidence: Each successful connection attempt actually results in the creation of two separate connections—one between the client and the proxy server, and another between the proxy server and the true destination.

notes.front: Why are some application-proxy gateways poorly suited to high-bandwidth or real-time applications?
notes.back: The firewall spends much more time reading and interpreting each packet.
notes.explanation: NIST ties this to the gateways’ “full packet awareness”.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.4 Application-Proxy Gateways, p. 16
notes.evidence: because of the “full packet awareness” of application-proxy gateways, the firewall spends much more time reading and interpreting each packet. Because of this, some of these gateways are poorly suited to high-bandwidth or real-time applications

notes.front: A firewall keeps a table of source and destination addresses, ports and connection state, and drops a packet claiming to belong to a connection it has no record of. Which filtering method is this?
notes.back: B: stateful inspection.
notes.choices:
A) Application-proxy gateway
B) Stateful inspection
C) Web application firewall
D) Dedicated proxy server
notes.choicesExplained: A creates two separate connections and inspects content. C protects web servers against web exploits. D relays application traffic with limited firewalling.
notes.explanation: Stateful inspection tracks each connection in a state table and blocks packets that deviate from the expected state.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.2 Stateful Inspection, p. 14
notes.evidence: stateful inspection keeps track of each connection in a state table. While the details of state table entries vary by firewall product, they typically include source IP address, destination IP address, port numbers, and connection state information.

notes.front: Where are dedicated proxy servers typically deployed, and why?
notes.back: Behind traditional firewall platforms, because their own firewalling capabilities are limited.
notes.explanation: The main firewall can hand traffic for a particular application to the matching proxy, which filters or logs it.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.5 Dedicated Proxy Servers, p. 17
notes.evidence: such as simply blocking traffic based on its source or destination, they are typically deployed behind traditional firewall platforms. Typically, a main firewall could accept inbound traffic, determine which application is being targeted, and hand off traffic to the appropriate proxy server (e.g., email proxy).

notes.front: Which kind of proxy server is most common today?
notes.back: Outbound proxy servers, most commonly web proxies.
notes.explanation: Web proxies are the commonest example NIST gives.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.5 Dedicated Proxy Servers, p. 17
notes.evidence: Most proxy servers now in use are outbound proxy servers, with the most common being HTTP proxies.

notes.front: A school wants staff web browsing to be filtered and logged, and pages everyone visits to load faster. Which device fits best?
notes.back: B: an outbound web proxy server with caching.
notes.choices:
A) A passive sensor on a spanning port
B) An outbound web proxy server with caching
C) A web application firewall in front of the school’s web server
D) A load balancer
notes.choicesExplained: A only watches a copy of traffic. C protects the school’s own web server from inbound attacks, not staff browsing. D spreads load across service instances.
notes.explanation: Outbound proxies filter or log users’ traffic, and caching frequently used pages reduces network traffic and improves response times.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.5 Dedicated Proxy Servers, p. 17
notes.evidence: Many organizations enable caching of frequently used web pages on the proxy to reduce network traffic and improve response times.

notes.front: An online shop’s web server keeps receiving database injection and cross-site scripting attempts. Which device, placed in front of the server, is built to inspect for these?
notes.back: C: a web application firewall.
notes.choices:
A) A cloud access security broker
B) A passive sensor
C) A web application firewall
D) A dedicated outbound proxy server
notes.choicesExplained: A governs users’ access to cloud services. B only watches copies of traffic. D handles users’ outbound traffic, not attacks on the shop’s server.
notes.explanation: NIST describes this class of firewall as inspecting for database injection, operating system command injection and cross-site scripting, and preventing inbound attacks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, Enhanced Firewall Capabilities, p. 19
notes.evidence: this class of firewalls can inspect threat vectors for SQL Injection, operating system (OS) command injections, and cross-site scripting attacks, as well as prevent inbound attacks.

notes.front: What was the primary function of the first generation of CASBs?
notes.back: Discovering the cloud resources enterprise users accessed, preventing or minimising unauthorised cloud use.
notes.explanation: Visibility into all the cloud resources users accessed was that generation’s contribution.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB), p. 17
notes.evidence: The primary function of the first generation of CASBs was the discovery of resources. They provided visibility into all of the cloud resources that the enterprise users accessed, thus preventing or minimizing the chances of shadow IT.

notes.front: A firm finds staff sharing files through unapproved SaaS apps and wants its data rules applied to its approved cloud apps too. Which tool fits?
notes.back: B: a cloud access security broker.
notes.choices:
A) A unified threat management appliance
B) A cloud access security broker
C) A load balancer
D) An application-proxy gateway for email
notes.choicesExplained: A combines perimeter functions in one box but is not described as governing cloud applications. C spreads load. D proxies one application protocol.
notes.explanation: CASBs show which cloud services staff use, curbing unauthorised cloud use, and today’s CASBs also extend on-premises security policies to cloud applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB), p. 17
notes.evidence: thus preventing or minimizing the chances of shadow IT. Shadow IT is the practice of some users using cloud applications that are not authorized by the enterprise IT management

notes.front: What is signature-based detection very effective at, and largely ineffective at?
notes.back: Effective at known threats; largely ineffective at previously unknown threats, evasion-disguised threats and many variants of known threats.
notes.explanation: Unknown threats, disguised threats and variants all fall outside the known patterns it compares.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 2.3.1 Signature-Based Detection, p. 18
notes.evidence: Signature-based detection is very effective at detecting known threats but largely ineffective at detecting previously unknown threats, threats disguised by the use of evasion techniques, and many variants of known threats.

notes.front: What is the major benefit of anomaly-based detection?
notes.back: It can be very effective at detecting previously unknown threats.
notes.explanation: It compares activity with normal behaviour rather than with known threats.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 2.3.2 Anomaly-Based Detection, p. 18
notes.evidence: The major benefit of anomaly-based detection methods is that they can be very effective at detecting previously unknown threats.

notes.front: What is the primary drawback of stateful protocol analysis?
notes.back: It is very resource-intensive.
notes.explanation: The analysis is complex, and tracking state for many simultaneous sessions adds overhead.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 2.3.3 Stateful Protocol Analysis, p. 20
notes.evidence: The primary drawback to stateful protocol analysis methods is that they are very resource-intensive because of the complexity of the analysis and the overhead involved in performing state tracking for many simultaneous sessions.

notes.front: Whose profiles does stateful protocol analysis rely on, compared with anomaly-based detection?
notes.back: Vendor-developed universal profiles of how protocols should be used, not host- or network-specific profiles.
notes.explanation: Stateful analysis judges traffic against how a protocol should work anywhere; anomaly detection judges it against how this network usually behaves.
notes.contrast: Anomaly-based detection uses profiles built from the monitored hosts’ or network’s own normal activity.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 2.3.3 Stateful Protocol Analysis, p. 19
notes.evidence: Unlike anomaly-based detection, which uses host or network-specific profiles, stateful protocol analysis relies on vendor-developed universal profiles that specify how particular protocols should and should not be used.

notes.front: An IDPS alerts because web traffic at the internet border is taking far more bandwidth than the profile it learnt during normal working weeks. Which detection method fired?
notes.back: D: anomaly-based detection.
notes.choices:
A) Signature-based detection
B) Packet filtering
C) Stateful protocol analysis
D) Anomaly-based detection
notes.choicesExplained: A matches known-threat patterns, not traffic volumes. C checks protocol behaviour against vendor profiles. B is a firewall filtering method, not an IDPS detection method.
notes.explanation: The alert compares current activity with a profile of normal activity built over time.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 2.3.2 Anomaly-Based Detection, p. 18
notes.evidence: The IDPS then uses statistical methods to compare the characteristics of current activity to thresholds related to the profile, such as detecting when Web activity comprises significantly more bandwidth than expected and alerting an administrator of the anomaly.

notes.front: What is the most common example of a pure packet filtering device?
notes.back: A network router that employs access control lists.
notes.explanation: Packet filtering is built into most operating systems and devices capable of routing.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.1 Packet Filtering, p. 12
notes.evidence: Packet filtering capabilities are built into most operating systems and devices capable of routing; the most common example of a pure packet filtering device is a network router that employs access control lists.

notes.front: To save money, a manager proposes loading the edge router with hundreds of complex filtering rules instead of buying a firewall. What does NIST warn?
notes.back: B: routers are meant for routing; complex filtering can overload the router’s processor.
notes.choices:
A) Routers cannot filter packets at all
B) Routers are meant for routing; complex filtering can overload the router’s processor
C) Routers must never use access control lists
D) The router would become a passive sensor
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: routers with ACLs are the commonest pure packet filters. C contradicts that. D confuses routing with IDPS placement.
notes.explanation: NIST’s planning advice is to use devices as they were intended to be used.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Firewall planning: use devices as they were intended, p. 35
notes.evidence: routers are meant to handle routing, not highly complex filtering, which can cause an excess burden on the router’s processor.

notes.front: Under NIST’s denial-of-service protection control, which capacity measure alongside priorities, quotas and partitioning helps counter flooding denial-of-service attacks?
notes.back: Load balancing.
notes.explanation: Managing capacity keeps enough capacity available to counter flooding attacks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-5 Denial-of-Service Protection, p. 323
notes.evidence: Managing capacity ensures that sufficient capacity is available to counter flooding attacks. Managing capacity includes establishing selected usage priorities, quotas, partitioning, or load balancing.

notes.front: A high-impact system must stay available even if one site fails. Which option does NIST list for such systems?
notes.back: C: fully redundant, load-balanced systems at alternate sites.
notes.choices:
A) A cold site with tape backups only
B) A single server with a passive sensor
C) Fully redundant, load-balanced systems at alternate sites
D) An outbound web proxy
notes.choicesExplained: A restores slowly and suits lower impact levels. B and D do nothing for availability after a site loss.
notes.explanation: NIST says strategies for high-impact systems should consider high availability and redundancy.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide, Contingency strategies and FIPS 199 impact levels, p. 20
notes.evidence: Strategies for high-impact information systems should consider highavailability and redundancy options in their design. Options may include fully redundant load balanced systems at alternate sites, data mirroring, and offsite database replication.

notes.front: Besides DLP tools, what are two measures NIST lists for preventing exfiltration of information?
notes.back: Traffic profile analysis for unexpected volumes or types; monitoring for steganography; penetration testing (any two).
notes.explanation: NIST’s boundary protection control lists data loss and data leakage prevention tools among several complementary techniques.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, SC-7 Boundary Protection, p. 327
notes.evidence: employing traffic profile analysis to detect deviations from the volume and types of traffic expected, call backs to command and control centers, conducting penetration testing, monitoring for steganography, disassembling and reassembling packet headers, and using data loss and data leakage prevention tools.

notes.front: A clinic worries that staff might email spreadsheets of patients’ PII outside the organisation. Which technology is designed to spot such transfers at the network boundary?
notes.back: D: data loss prevention.
notes.choices:
A) A load balancer
B) A spanning port
C) Stateful protocol analysis
D) Data loss prevention
notes.choicesExplained: A spreads load. B gives a sensor a copy of switch traffic but decides nothing. C checks protocol behaviour, not whether the content is PII.
notes.explanation: NIST names DLP as an example of automated tools monitoring PII at network boundaries for unusual or suspicious transfers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-122, Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of PII, Information System Monitoring (SI-4), p. 31
notes.evidence: Organizations can employ automated tools to monitor PII internally or at network boundaries for unusual or suspicious transfers or events. An example is the use of data loss prevention technologies.

notes.front: What are two trade-offs NIST’s firewall guide gives for a UTM?
notes.back: It must have every feature needed for all objectives, and it needs enough processing power and memory to handle every task.
notes.explanation: Against these, one system responsible for several objectives reduces complexity.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.8 Unified Threat Management (UTM), p. 19
notes.evidence: deploying a UTM reduces complexity by making a single system responsible for multiple security objectives, but it also requires that the UTM have all the desired features to meet every one of the objectives. Another tradeoff is in performance: a single system handling multiple tasks has to have enough resources

notes.front: A branch office wants one box to manage instead of a separate firewall, anti-malware gateway and probe detector. What does NIST say about choosing a UTM?
notes.back: D: there are pros and cons; some organisations favour a UTM, others several firewalls.
notes.choices:
A) A UTM is always better than separate devices
B) Separate devices are always better than a UTM
C) UTMs are not able to run a firewall
D) There are pros and cons; some organisations favour a UTM, others several firewalls
notes.choicesExplained: A and B harden what NIST leaves as a balance. C is wrong: a firewall is a typical UTM component.
notes.explanation: A UTM simplifies policy, but it must have every feature and enough resources for every task.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1.8 Unified Threat Management (UTM), p. 19
notes.evidence: Some organizations will find the balance favors a UTM, while other organizations will use multiple firewalls at the same location in their network.
